rv.q: But there’s compassion and even tenderness running through this play that make it one of his best.
Neil LaBute's new play about the damage that casual cruelty can inflict on relationships is a thoughtful, well-crafted work that benefits from strong performances.

Reasons to Be Happy is an engrossing if less impactful companion piece that again tempers LaBute’s sardonic side by allowing a glimmer of compassion for people who seem incapable of sustaining lasting connections.
"Reasons to Be Happy" has its improbabilities and rough edges, but what ultimately emerges is a winning sympathy for the difficulties of life and love.
But its contemplative dialogue is often overwritten and meandering.
If, however, Fischer wanted a dynamic, meaty role for her professional stage debut, she's about five years and one play too late.
